question: For \(x\) real, the inequality \(1\le\lvert x-2\rvert\le7\) is equivalent to:
solution:
The quantity \(\lvert x-2\rvert\) is the distance from \(x\) to \(2\) on the number line. That distance must be at least \(1\) and at most \(7\).

To the left of \(2\), the allowed points run from \(2-7=-5\) to \(2-1=1\). To the right, they run from \(2+1=3\) to \(2+7=9\). Every point in these intervals has an allowed distance, and every point outside them violates one of the bounds.

All four endpoints are included because both inequalities allow equality. Thus
\[
-5\le x\le1
\quad\text{or}\quad
3\le x\le9,
\]
which is choice D.

edges.reason: The actual number-line criterion checks an origin, a designated direction and a unit. A designated positive direction is an orientation convention; it does not require the full signed-number classification or negative contexts asserted by Gemini.
edges.scope: Origin, designated orientation and unit as the three structural elements of a number line

edges.reason: Absolute value is defined as the distance from a point to the origin. That definition presupposes a number line with an origin and a unit length, which give distance its meaning.
edges.scope: geometric meaning of absolute value as distance to origin

edges.reason: The distance-from-origin definition refers to the point representing the number, so number-to-point interpretation is a component of this geometric criterion.
The target explicitly asks for the equal absolute values of opposite numbers; the opposite-number relation is part of that assertion.
edges.scope: Criterion: opposites have equal absolute values

edges.reason: A signed numerical inequality expresses an order relation, so the meaning of greater/less is part of interpreting it.
The plotted object is the set of all values making an inequality true; solution and solution-set meanings are required.

Both sign-interval and geometric routes use the absolute-value quantity, distinct from an unsigned affine expression. Absolute magnitude is shared meaning. Sign rewriting and affine inequality solving belong only to the sign-interval route; a single-distance bound can instead be read directly on the number line.
edges.scope: absolute value as a nonnegative distance
